mappings.note: MISFILED chemistry (10SCIENCE5qa). K (19) with Cl (17): the formula follows from valency and position (C 1.1), but the electron-dot structure and naming the bond ionic is compound formation by electron transfer (C 1.3). Both halves are assessed, so both cited.
Order Mg, Ca, K, Ge, Ga by increasing metallic character -- a two-axis periodicity trend. C 1.1 is the only competency covering periodic trends; CG 1 has no LOs.

Identify a soft reactive metal, the metal in limestone and the liquid metal, then order them by reactivity. Identification is by group membership and the ordering is the down-group reactivity trend -- C 1.1 throughout, with no reaction written, so not C 1.3.
Five property clues (kerosene storage, variable valency, tetravalent carbon, Z=2 inert gas, anodising) each resolved to a position in the table. Locating elements from properties is C 1.1.

Group 2 period 3 element burning to a basic oxide. Identification and configuration are C 1.1; the two balanced equations (burning in air, oxide dissolving in water) and the electron-dot structure of the oxide are C 1.3. Cited together because a C 1.1-only mapping would miss three of the five parts.
X (17) and Y (20) forming a divalent halide. Positions and the metal/non-metal/metalloid classification are C 1.1; the nature of Y's oxide, the bonding and the dot structure are C 1.3.
For Z = 10, 20, 7, 14: identity, group, period, configuration and valency. Every part is configuration-to-position, C 1.1.

The jumbled-ladder figure is not printed, but the stored answer shows both parts are ordering elements by atomic number and then grouping them -- exactly C 1.1, so it is mapped rather than left as an unreadable figure item.
Element crossword: each clue is a property-to-element identification (group 14 canning metal, halogen, alkali metal in kerosene, first metalloid). Identification from periodic position is C 1.1.
Eka-silicon and Eka-aluminium: their modern names, group, period, metal/non-metal class and valence electrons. Predicted-element placement, C 1.1.
Given four stated trends, pick the most electropositive, most electronegative, smallest and metalloid among Z = 3 to 9. Applying periodicity trends, C 1.1.

Yellow solid showing catenation and allotropy (sulphur). Identity, configuration and position are C 1.1; the balanced thermal-decomposition equation for ferrous sulphate and the acidic nature of the oxides are C 1.3.

Group-15 diatomic element combining with hydrogen to give ammonia. Identifying nitrogen and counting its valence electrons is C 1.1; the two electron-dot structures and naming the bonds covalent is C 1.3.
Which group slotted into Mendeleev's table without disturbing it (the noble gases) and why. A property of the classification scheme, C 1.1.
Account of Mendeleev's method and how he arrived at the Periodic Law -- the fullest statement of the classification competency, C 1.1.
Which of Z = 9, 17, 24, 30, 35, 45 share a group -- valence-electron count from configuration, C 1.1.
Three sets to order by decreasing atomic size, mixing a down-group and an across-period case. Atomic-size periodicity, C 1.1.
Name and configuration of the second alkali metal -- group membership to identity, C 1.1.
What Mg, Ca and Sr configurations share (two valence electrons) -- the defining feature of a group, C 1.1.
Members of the alkaline earth family and which is radioactive -- group membership, C 1.1. Radioactivity is incidental; the frame has no nuclear competency.
Whether chlorine's two isotopes need separate slots -- the isotope problem is a classification question about what the table orders by, C 1.1.
Mass number 35 with 18 neutrons gives Z = 17, hence group 17 period 3. Atomic composition to position, C 1.1.
How metallic character varies down a group and across a period -- the bare trend, C 1.1.
Name three metalloids -- the metal/non-metal boundary of the table, C 1.1.
What all elements in boron's PERIOD share (same number of shells). Paired with the next item, which asks the group version; both are C 1.1 because the frame draws no group/period distinction.
What all elements in fluorine's GROUP share (seven valence electrons). Same competency as the period version above, C 1.1.
Configuration of the period-3 group-17 element -- position back to configuration, the reverse of the usual direction but the same C 1.1 idea.
Basic configuration difference between groups 1 and 2 -- one vs two valence electrons, C 1.1.
Three group-17 elements in periods 2, 3, 4; given Y has 7 valence electrons, deduce X and Z. Tests that valence-electron count is constant down a group, C 1.1.
Y (Z=3) with A (Z=17): give the formula. Valency from configuration, C 1.1. Bonding is not asked, so C 1.3 is not cited here although it is on the fuller versions of this item.
Two more family members for fluorine, calcium and carbon -- group membership, C 1.1.
Classify four sets as a group or a period -- the distinction between the two axes of the table, C 1.1.
From MgO deduce MgCl2 -- transferring a valency between compounds, which C 1.1 covers as compound formation from valency. No equation or reaction, so not C 1.3.
Valency expected from configuration 2,8,7 -- valence electrons to valency, C 1.1.
What two elements in the same period share (shell count) -- C 1.1.
Identify the element with configuration 2,8,6 and name its family -- configuration to identity to group name, C 1.1.
How the tendency to gain electrons changes down a group -- the electronegativity/non-metallic trend, C 1.1.
Why properties recur after 8, 8, 18, 18, 18, 32 -- periodicity explained by shell-filling capacity, the heart of C 1.1.
Pick the non-metals from four configurations -- valence electrons to metallic character, C 1.1.
17p/18n and 17p/20n are both chlorine -- recognising isotopes from subatomic counts, the classification-relevant sense of isotope, C 1.1.

Identify elements from a golden-yellow flame, a whitewash oxide and the chlorophyll constituent, then order by metallic character. Despite the chlorophyll clue this is not a biology item -- it is element identification plus a metallic-character trend, C 1.1.
Configurations of Mg and Al and the period they share, with a reason -- shell count determines period, C 1.1.

Table fragment is garbled in the stem, but the stored answer shows all three parts are atomic number and atomic-size comparisons across a period and down a group -- C 1.1, determinable without the table.
Calcium (Z=20): metal or not, size against potassium, formula of its chloride. Three periodicity/valency deductions, C 1.1.
Mass 35 with 18 neutrons: atomic number, configuration, group, period and valency. The fuller version of qid:85545 and the same competency, C 1.1.
Order Li, Na, K by decreasing metallic character -- down-group metallic trend, C 1.1.
X (12) and Y (16): configurations and shared period are C 1.1; predicting an ionic bond between them and justifying it is C 1.3. Cited together because the bond question is the weightier half.
Configuration 2,8,3 to atomic number, group and period -- C 1.1.
What same-period elements share, and why chlorine and bromine are in one group -- the period and group criteria side by side, C 1.1.
Period 3 group 2: valence electrons, metal or not, name, formula of oxide. All four follow from position, C 1.1; no reaction is written so C 1.3 is not cited.
Arrange the second-period elements in table order, name the largest and smallest atom, and explain why radius changes across a period. Atomic-size periodicity with its cause, C 1.1.
Why C, N, O and F sit in period 2, and why group 17 is monovalent -- shell count and valence-electron count respectively, both C 1.1.
Why chlorine is more electronegative than sulphur -- across-period electronegativity trend, C 1.1.
Of Z = 9, 11, 17, which two behave alike -- F and Cl share a group. Group membership from configuration, C 1.1.
For Z = 5, 7, 10 give the group-13 and group-15 members and the shared period, with reasons -- C 1.1.

Two reasons noble gases were discovered late -- their chemical inertness and low abundance, i.e. the properties that define that group. C 1.1 rather than a history-of-science code: CG 6 is Indian contributions and CG 7 is current frontiers, neither of which this is.
For Z = 7, 8, 9: positions, decreasing size, and the most reactive with a reason. Three across-period trends, C 1.1.
Across period 2 predict the most electronegative, most electropositive, the noble gas and the element of organic chemistry. Applying trends, C 1.1.
List four properties that show periodicity -- names the trends themselves, C 1.1.
From X = 2, Y = 2,6, Z = 2,8,2 identify period, group, valency and metal/non-metal status. Configuration-to-position throughout, C 1.1.
